title: The RLC Circuit That Peaked Instead of Filtering
featured_title: THE RLC CIRCUIT THAT PEAKED INSTEAD OF FILTERING
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

presentation.challenge: Both reactive components looked like opposition. At resonance, they canceled and the current doubled the protection limit.

practice.primary_question: Why can the current in a series RLC circuit peak at resonance even though both the inductor and capacitor have reactance?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Adding the magnitudes of inductive and capacitive reactance at resonance instead of recognizing that their signed reactances cancel.

case_dna.target_misconception: Inductive and capacitive reactance always add as positive opposition, so adding both components must reduce current.
case_dna.why_plausible: Students often calculate |XL| and |XC| correctly but forget that inductive and capacitive reactances have opposite signs in series impedance.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: At about 50.3 Hz, XL and XC are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so they cancel and the series impedance falls to R = 20 Ω, producing 0.50 A from 10 V rms.
case_dna.corrected_model: Use Z = R + j(XL - XC). At series resonance XL = XC, the reactive part is zero, |Z| = R, and current reaches its maximum value V/R.

problem_statement: A 10 V rms source drives a series RLC circuit with R = 20 Ω, L = 100 mH, and C = 100 µF. The branch is protected for 0.25 A. The technician assumes the inductor and capacitor both add opposition, but near 50.3 Hz the current rises to 0.50 A and protection operates. Find the resonance condition, explain why the reactive terms do not add, and choose a safe correction while keeping the source, L, and C unchanged.
fixed_constraints: Current at resonance must not exceed 0.25 A

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The 'extra reactance' made the current larger, not smaller.
gates.prompt: Why did the branch current peak when both an inductor and capacitor were present?

gates.label: Theory
gates.heading: Choose the model before sweeping frequency

options.label: XL and XC add as positive opposition, so current must fall
options.reason: Series impedance uses j(XL - XC), not the sum of the reactance magnitudes. The signs matter.

options.label: At resonance XL = XC, so the reactive terms cancel and only R limits current
options.reason: This is the series-resonance condition. With zero net reactance, |Z| = R and current is maximized.

options.label: The capacitor becomes a permanent short circuit at 50 Hz
options.reason: The capacitor still has finite reactance. The peak occurs because its reactance cancels the inductor's reactance, not because XC becomes zero.

options.label: A 0.50 A reading must mean the source voltage doubled
options.reason: The stated 10 V rms source produces 0.50 A when the impedance magnitude falls to 20 Ω.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the current at resonance
gates.prompt: If the reactive terms cancel at resonance, what current (A) does a 10 V rms source drive through R = 20 Ω?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Sweep through resonance
gates.result: Near 50.3 Hz, the series current reaches 0.50 A. The reactive terms cancel and the 20 Ω resistance sets the impedance magnitude.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Find the resonant frequency
gates.prompt: Use f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) with L = 0.1 H and C = 100 µF. Enter f0 in Hz.
gates.success: f0 ≈ 50.33 Hz. At this frequency XL ≈ XC ≈ 31.6 Ω, so Z ≈ 20 Ω and I ≈ 0.50 A.
gates.hint: Convert 100 µF to 100 × 10⁻⁶ F before using the resonance formula.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The impedance components show why the current peaks

cards.text: At the same frequency, XC = 1/(2πfC) ≈ 31.6 Ω.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the impedance review
report: C1. The branch contains 20 Ω resistance, 100 mH inductance, and 100 µF capacitance in series.
C2. Near 50.3 Hz, the magnitudes of XL and XC are each about 31.6 Ω.
C3. Because both components have reactance, their magnitudes add and keep current below the 0.25 A protection limit.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: C2 is numerically consistent with the resonance condition.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: C3 ignores the opposite signs of inductive and capacitive reactance. At resonance they cancel rather than add.

evidence_choices.label: XL ≈ XC and Z ≈ 20 + j0 Ω at 50.3 Hz
evidence_choices.reason: This directly proves that the reactive terms cancel and the current is limited mainly by R.

evidence_choices.label: The source is 10 V rms
evidence_choices.reason: The source value is needed for current, but it does not explain the resonance mechanism.

evidence_choices.label: The circuit contains a capacitor
evidence_choices.reason: A capacitor alone does not prove resonance; the equality and opposite signs of XL and XC do.

correction.template: At resonance the reactive terms cancel, so the impedance is about {resistance} Ω and the source current rises to {current} A.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Keep resonance current at or below 0.25 A
gates.constraint: Keep the 10 V rms source, 100 mH inductor, and 100 µF capacitor unchanged.

options.label: Increase total series resistance to at least 40 Ω
options.reason: At resonance, I = V/R. To keep I ≤ 0.25 A, R ≥ 10/0.25 = 40 Ω.

options.label: Reduce total series resistance to 10 Ω
options.reason: At resonance this would increase current to 1 A.

options.label: Keep 20 Ω because XL and XC each exceed 30 Ω
options.reason: At resonance those reactances cancel, leaving 20 Ω as the limiting impedance.

options.label: Increase the source voltage to improve filtering
options.reason: Higher voltage increases the resonant current and worsens the protection problem.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the resonance-current rule
gates.prompt: A series RLC circuit is exactly at resonance with an 8 V rms source and 40 Ω total resistance. What is the current?

options.label: 0.20 A
options.reason: At series resonance the net reactance is zero, so I = V/R = 8/40 = 0.20 A.

options.label: 0 A
options.reason: Resonance minimizes series impedance; it does not open the circuit.

options.label: 5 A
options.reason: The correct relation is 8 V / 40 Ω = 0.20 A.

options.label: Cannot be known without L and C
options.reason: Once the circuit is stated to be at series resonance, L and C cancel in the net reactance and V/R determines current.

gates.explanation: At ideal series resonance, XL = XC and the impedance reduces to the total series resistance.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the resonance analysis
gates.confirmation: I confirm that series RLC impedance uses the signed difference XL - XC and that current is maximized when those reactances cancel.

items.label: What tripped protection
items.value: Series resonance reduced the impedance to about 20 Ω, producing 0.50 A.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Inductive and capacitive reactances have opposite signs and cancel at resonance.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use Z = R + j(XL - XC); at resonance, |Z| = R and I = V/R.

seo.seo_title: Series RLC Resonance: Why Current Peaks | FE E-021
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-021: a 10 V series RLC circuit reaches 0.50 A near 50.3 Hz. Calculate resonance and see why XL and XC cancel.
seo.excerpt: An inductor and capacitor do not always add opposition. At series resonance, their reactances cancel and current can reach its maximum value.
seo.direct_answer: In a series RLC circuit, impedance is Z = R + j(XL - XC). At resonance XL = XC, so the reactive terms cancel and the impedance magnitude becomes R. With 10 V rms and 20 Ω, the resonant current is 0.50 A.

faqs.q: What happens to current at series resonance?
faqs.a: The net reactance becomes zero, the impedance magnitude is minimized to the series resistance, and current reaches its maximum value for a fixed source voltage.

faqs.q: What is the resonant frequency for 100 mH and 100 µF?
Do inductive and capacitive reactance add at resonance?
faqs.a: Their magnitudes are equal, but their signs are opposite, so they cancel in the series impedance.
